Thank you for submitting your work entitled "AMPA-type glutamate receptors on oligodendrocyte precursors modulate development of oligodendrocytes and myelin" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor.

The reviewers appreciated that your exploration of the issue of how neuronal activity and glutamate signaling regulate development of the oligodendrocyte lineage is timely and important. Unfortunately, however, they found the interpretation of the effects of inactivation of AMPA receptors gluR2/3 on oligodendrocyte maturation, myelin/myelinated axons, and AMPA currents somewhat preliminary. The reviews are summed below, but the main, shared concerns include:

1) Whether the transient decrease in CC1+ oligodendrocytes arises due to a delay in differentiation or a decrease in survival.

2) Whether myelination is truly decreased/delayed; suggestions for further analyses are to examine parameters of myelin internodes and to better quantify the EM data.

3) Whether in the absence of GluA2, alterations in AMPA current are due to AMPAR inhibition or to altered AMPAR signaling. In line with this, reviewer 2 had concerns that AMPAR-mediated current still remains in the double knockouts, potentially obscuring some effects of AMPAR inhibition, and thus producing only a modest change.

Because your study requires additional amendments that would likely take longer than a few months, we will have to reject the manuscript at this time.

Reviewer #1:

In the manuscript by Kougioumtzidou et al., the authors set out to investigate whether AMPAR signaling has a role in regulating oligodendrocyte development in vivo (first demonstration). They show that oligodendrocyte precursor cells express 3 of 4 known AMPAR subunits (Gria2-4). They then proceed to analyze oligodendrocyte development in Gria3 KOs, SOX10-conditional Gria2 KOs and Gria2/3 double KOs. They show that there are no effects on oligodendrocyte development in the individual KOs, even though AMPAR signaling is affected. However, the double KOs show an early, but transient decrease/delay in differentiated oligodendrocyte density during development (P14), which returns to normal by P21, and they conclude that AMPAR signaling regulates oligodendrocyte differentiation. The mice display a similar decrease in the number of myelinated axons in the double KOs and conclude that AMPAR signaling also regulates myelination. Since glutamatergic signaling through AMPAR is thought to be a major form of communication between neurons and oligodendrocyte precursors, and the resulting effects of this communication on oligodendrocyte development are still largely unknown, the topic of this manuscript is timely and highly important to the field. However, the work presented falls far short of accomplishing its aim and does little to move the field forward. Major concerns are outlined below.

1) The authors illustrate that a good deal of AMPAR-mediated current (~50%) still remains in the double KOs, which may obscure some effects of AMPAR inhibition. Perhaps because of this the effects demonstrated in this manuscript as a result of the double KOs are modest and do not add any mechanistic insight to what is already known.

2) As the authors state, the fact that there is no change in OP densities/proliferation in Gria2/3 KOs argues against the decrease in CC1+ OLs being due to a delay in developmental OL differentiation, but more for a decrease in OL survival, which the authors were unable to quantify. Not only does this leave the work incomplete, but it also makes it improper to conclude that AMPARs "modulate the development of OLs" when the effects seen could be a survival issue.

3) The authors show a reduction in myelinated neurons and suggest that OL differentiation and therefore myelination is delayed. However, they also present g-ratios that are unaffected. If developmental myelination is indeed delayed the KOs would show increased g-ratios since the myelin would begin to form later than controls. No change in g-ratios suggests other possibilities such as a survival issue of the OLs (see #2), or even the possibility that myelin internode lengths are shorter. Other studies have shown that OLs make shorter myelin sheaths upon inhibition of neuronal activity and decreased glutamate signaling (Hines et al. 2015. Nat Neurosci. 18:683-689; Mensch et al. 2015. Nat Neurosci. 18:628-630., Etxeberria et al. 2016. J Neurosci. 36:6037-6948.), therefore, it is a likely possibility that the decrease in myelinated axons observed by the authors is due to a similar change in myelin dynamics. An in-depth analysis of the myelin internodes (length and number/OL) is required to ascertain the full effect of AMPR function. Further investigation is necessary.

4) It is known that the GluA2 subunit makes AMPARs impermeable to Ca+2, therefore knocking out Gria2 will lead to increased Ca+2 signaling and changes the whole nature of AMPAR signaling. Moreover, the authors suspect that the remaining AMPAR-mediated currents are due to homotetramers of GluA4, but these are likely never normally produced in OPCs and may not reveal any meaningful signaling effects. Ultimately it is not clear whether the effects the authors are studying are due to AMPAR inhibition or to altered AMPAR signaling.

Reviewer #2:

Oligodendrocyte lineage cells express glutamate receptors. Nevertheless, the functional significance of the expression of the distinct types of glutamate receptors by these cells has not been completely characterized. In the current study Kougioumtzidou and colleagues sought to identify the role that AMPA receptors play in oligodendrocyte lineage cells. They found that kainate-induced current is mediated by the expression of the AMPA receptors GluA2, GluA3 and GluA4 in oligodendrocyte lineage cells. In addition, these investigators genetically inactivated GluA2 and GluA3, individually and together, to determine the functional significance of this expression. The investigators took advantage of pre-existing GluA3 null mutant mice, as well as a GluA2 conditional mutant mouse line that they combined with a Sox10-Cre driver to promote recombination in oligodendrocyte lineage cells. This resulted in mice in which GluA3 expression was omitted from all cells, whereas GluA2 was specifically eliminated from oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and the expression of GluA4 remained intact. Although the individual mutants were unaffected in a detectable way, the double mutant mice exhibited partial blockage of kainate-induced current in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. In agreement with previous studies, the authors found that the partial blockage of the kainate- induced current in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells did not affect these cells in any identifiable manner. Interestingly, however, the authors demonstrate that the combined ablation of GluA2 and GluA3 resulted in an approximate twenty percent reduction in the number of mature oligodendrocytes at early postnatal ages that correlates with mild hypomyelination. Overall, this is an interesting and well-done study that adds to our growing understanding of the role that glutamate signaling plays in oligodendrocyte lineage cells.

1) Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells are highly proliferative. Since the authors use a conditional approach to the inactivation of GluA2, it is likely that not all OPCs have both alleles of GluA2 inactivated. It is possible that over time OPCs with the conditional inactivation of GluA2 are selected against, which might explain the observed recovery in older animals. A more detailed examination of this would be very informative: is there a higher percentage of WT GluA2 OPCs in older double-mutant animals?

2) A very interesting finding of this report is that AMPA receptors are important for differentiated, myelinating oligodendrocytes. Nevertheless, in my view this finding is not highlighted sufficiently. A proposed role for GluA2 and GluA3 in myelinating oligodendrocytes should be discussed.

3) Does the percent of myelinated axons recover to normal levels in adult animals? This data should be included in Figure 8.

Reviewer #3:

Kougioumtzidou et al., submit "AMPA-type glutamate receptors on oligodendrocyte precursors modulate development of oligodendrocytes and myelin" for consideration at eLife. This work centres on to topic of how neuronal activity regulates development of the oligodendrocyte lineage. This general area will be of broad interest to the readership of eLife in large part because changes to oligodendrocyte development and myelination help regulate or fine tune neural circuit function and behaviour – the latter shown in a very elegant study by the Richardson lab. In this study, the authors address how glutamate signalling directly impacts oligodendrocyte development in vivo (a long-standing question), with a focus on AMPAR mediated function. Although one might argue that the authors did not address how AMPAR function in its entirety affects oligodendrocyte development (disrupting gluR2 and gluR3, but not gluR4, which is also expressed in the OL lineage), they do see a clear phenotype in vivo, and this is of interest in and of itself. However, at the moment I think that the manuscript would benefit greatly from some additional work to allay a few concerns, and to strengthen some of the conclusions drawn.

Validation of gria3 global mutant as reasonable "control" background. The authors go to some lengths to highlight the importance of a conditional targeting approach, whereby AMPRA mediated signalling/ function is disrupted specifically in oligodendrocytes. They achieve this is by targeting gluR2 function using floxed alleles of gria2 and a sox10-cre, which seems sufficiently faithful to the oligodendrocyte lineage in the CNS. However, all experiments are done on a background of lack of GluR3 function, i.e. a germline gria3 mutant mouse. Indeed all "controls" are gria3 mutant. The authors do show that gria3 mutants exhibit no change in PDGFRa expressing oligodendrocyte precursors (or their proliferation) or CC1 expressing mature oligodendrocytes, but only one stage is examined, and no further tests are carried out. In addition to the possibility of gria3 mutant oligodendrocytes having defects at other stages or at other times, these mutants will surely have compensation for glur3 loss by expression/ regulation of other GluR subunit isoforms and disruption to neural circuit function that could potentially confound analysis of myelination. It would be reassuring to see further analyses of gria3 mutants compared to controls, e.g. additional stages, electron microscopy (see last point below), to allay concerns that its use as a control is not confounding.

Mechanism by which reduction in oligodendrocyte number is manifest

It is certainly interesting that there is a reduction (albeit transient) in mature oligodendrocyte number and enpp6 expressing cell number, but the follow-up analyses as to how this comes to be come across as being a little preliminary. The authors report no significant change in PDGFRa density, but there is a stage at which there is a trend reduction in double mutants with a p value of 0.06. Could an increase in "n" unmask a phenotype? The analyses of cell death are also unsatisfying, given the importance of clarifying the role for AMPAR in the cell lineage. The use of additional marker(s) for cell death would be important. Is there no constitutive oligodendrocyte lineage cell death in actual wildtype animals at any of the stages examined?

Fewer synapses exist in double mutants. The conclusion that oligodendrocyte precursors have fewer synapses per cell is an inference based on the physiological analyses. Although a reasonable inference, to provide independent evidence in support of this conclusion would be good. Could the authors try to visualise synapse number in OPs, e.g. with a presynaptic marker at least, or ideally with a pre and post-synaptic marker together with NG2, enpp6 etc.?

Electron microscopy analyses could be better quantified. It is important that the electron microscopy data support the observations of a decrease in oligodendrocyte number, whereby the authors observe a corresponding decrease in relative number of axons that are myelinated. It would be helpful to assess axonal sizes and distributions in the mutants as well, and ideally compare with controls that were not gria3 null. Comparison of gria3 mutants to control littermates would suffice.

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted for further consideration.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Signalling through AMPA receptors on oligodendrocyte precursors promotes oligodendrocyte survival and myelination" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Marianne Bronner (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor and three reviewers.

The three reviewers agreed that the manuscript is greatly improved. They applaud your success in making the AMPAR triple KO's that have an abrogation of almost all AMPAR-related currents in the oligodendrocyte lineage. They consider your finding that the disruption to AMPAR signaling in oligodendrocytes causing their increased cell death is sufficient to explain the subsequent deficits in myelination, a strong and exciting addition to the field.

There are a few remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, mostly textual, as outlined below:

1) Title: From your data, it seems as though the role of AMPAR signaling in OPCs/ immature ENPP6 expressing OLs is to control the number of oligodendrocytes that can be maintained and employed for myelination or discarded, if unnecessary. The title stating "survival and myelination" implies two separate roles; "survival and thus myelination" would be a more apt reference to your findings.

2) Data on the cell death phenotype (Figures 7 and 10): To support this finding, it would be helpful to understand the proportion of cells that are caspase positive in the population examined in your analyses, to understand what level of possible overproduction/regulation by activity is at play in the system. Even though the numbers are likely not absolute, if you thought it reasonable, adding these numbers would further bolster your case.

3) Discussion:

A) The lack of an obvious role for AMPAR in regulating myelin sheath number, length, thickness per cell is of great interest. However, it may be misleading to state that this result mirrors observations that in vitro sheath length is not regulated by activity. Indeed, evidence from the Fields lab shows that inactive axon sheath lengths are significantly shorter on silent (vesicular release impaired) axons (Wake et al., Nat Comm), and similarly, in vivo in zebrafish (Koudelka et al., Curr Biol.) The AMPAR negative data may instead imply that control of sheath length is mediated by other glutamatergic receptors, or by other signals, and should be noted.

B) It may be inaccurate to state that reduction of activity did not affect OL numbers in zebrafish with reduced neuronal activity; a modest reduction in cell number was seen with reduced activity, and conversely an increase with increase in activity (Mensch et al., Nat Neurosci). It would be helpful to address control of cell number at specific stages of OL development, given the extensive work on this topic and recent work identifying other possible regulators of OPC proliferation (Venkatesh et al., Cell). Discuss whether the proportion regulated by AMPAR reflects cells that have transitioned from pure OPCs to ENPP6-expressing stage and are faced with an activity-regulated decision to commit to myelination, thus a time-specific role for AMPAR in the OL lineage.

claims.claim: The kainate-evoked current density was approximately 47% less in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: Normalizing the amplitude of the maximum kainate-evoked current at –63 mV to the cell size (assessed as membrane capacitance) revealed a significant (~47%) reduction in the current density for Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls (p<10–4, Student's t-test; Figure 5B), indicating that the number of AMPARs expressed on the cell surface was decreased in Gria3null2–/– mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In both Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ OPs, kainate-evoked currents were blocked by approximately 80% in the presence of GYKI-52466.
claims.source: In both Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ OPs, kainate-evoked currents were blocked by ~80% in the presence of GYKI (Figure 5A,C), confirming that most of the kainate-evoked current is AMPAR-mediated under our experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: There was no evidence for up-regulation of Gria1 mRNA in Gria3null2–/– subcortical white matter relative to Gria3null2+/+.
claims.source: However, by ISH we found no evidence for up-regulation of Gria1 mRNA in Gria3null2–/– SCWM relative to Gria3null2+/+ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The majority of AMPARs formed in Gria3null2–/– OPs are probably homo-tetramers of GluA4.
claims.source: Thus, the majority of AMPAR formed in Gria3null2–/– OPs are probably homo-tetramers of GluA4.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of Gria1 upregulation and the presence of GluA4.

claims.claim: Neither the membrane resistance nor the capacitance of Gria3null2–/– OPs at –63 mV were different from Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: Neither the membrane resistance (Rm) nor the capacitance (Cm) of Gria3null2–/– OPs at –63 mV were different from Gria3null2+/+ controls (for Rm, p=0.16, Mann-Whitney test and for Cm, p=0.13, Student's t-test; Figure 5D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the INa density between Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in the INa density between Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ controls (p=0.72, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 5G), suggesting that altering AMPAR signalling does not regulate the expression of voltage-gated sodium channels.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: AMPAR signalling does not much affect the membrane properties of oligodendrocyte precursors.
claims.source: We conclude that AMPAR signalling does not much affect the membrane properties of OPs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The amplitude of evoked EPSCs appeared the same in Gria3null2–/– and their Gria3null2+/– controls.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the amplitude of the evoked EPSCs appeared the same in Gria3null2–/– and their Gria3null2+/– controls (p=0.37, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 6A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The mean amplitude of individual RR-evoked EPSCs was not reduced in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/– controls or Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: Consistent with the minimal stimulation-evoked EPSC data, the mean amplitude of individual RR-evoked EPSCs was not reduced in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/– controls or Gria3null2+/+ controls (p=0.32, one-way ANOVA; Figure 6C,D)
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The frequency of RR-evoked EPSCs was approximately 70% less in Gria3null2–/– than in Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: However, the frequency of RR-evoked EPSCs was ~70% less in Gria3null2–/– than in Gria3null2+/+ controls, and was reduced to an intermediate frequency in Gria3null2+/– controls (p=2×10–4, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc test; Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: There was no difference in PPR of Gria3null2–/– OPs versus Gria3null2+/+ OPs.
claims.source: There was no difference in PPR of Gria3null2–/– OPs versus Gria3null2+/+ OPs (p=0.95, Student's t-test; Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The reduction in EPSC frequency is not due to a change in presynaptic glutamate release but rather because fewer active synapses are formed or maintained in Gria3null2–/– mice.
claims.source: This suggests that the reduction in EPSC frequency is not due to a change in presynaptic glutamate release but rather because fewer active synapses are formed or maintained in Gria3null2–/– mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the paired-pulse ratio data.

claims.claim: There was a approximately 22% reduction in the density of oligodendrocytes at P7 in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: There was a ~22% reduction in the density of OLs at P7 and a ~27% reduction at P14 in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls (p=0.018 at P7; p=0.001 at P14, t–tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction; Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: There was a approximately 27% reduction in the density of oligodendrocytes at P14 in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls.
claims.source: There was a ~22% reduction in the density of OLs at P7 and a ~27% reduction at P14 in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls (p=0.018 at P7; p=0.001 at P14, t–tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction; Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: By P21 and P70, the difference in oligodendrocyte density between Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ was no longer significant.
claims.source: By P21 (p=0.14) and P70 (p=0.48, Mann-Whitney test with Holm-Bonferroni correction) this difference was no longer significant.
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: There was a approximately 26% reduction in the density of Enpp6+ newly-differentiated oligodendrocytes in Gria3null2–/– mice compared to their Gria3null2+/+ littermates at P14.
claims.source: This revealed a ~26% reduction of Enpp6+ newly-differentiated OLs in Gria3null2–/– mice compared to their Gria3null2+/+ littermates (p=0.004, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 7C,D)
claims.evidence: Supported by ISH data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in the density of OPs in Gria3null2–/– subcortical white matter compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls at P3, P7, P14, P21, and P70.
claims.source: We found no significant differences in the density of OPs in Gria3null2–/– SCWM compared to Gria3null2+/+ controls (p=0.6 at P3; p=0.85 at P7; p=0.07 at P14; p>0.99 at P21 and p=0.76 at P70, t–test or Mann-Whitney test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; Figure 7E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The fraction of Pdgfra+ OPs that incorporated EdU was not detectably different in Gria3null2–/– versus Gria3null2+/+ subcortical white matter at P3, P7, P14, and P70.
claims.source: The fraction of Pdgfra+ OPs that incorporated EdU ('labelling index') was not detectably different in Gria3null2–/– versus Gria3null2+/+ SCWM at any age examined (p=0.69 at P3; p=0.69 at P7; p=0.7 at P14; p=0.34 at P70, Mann-Whitney tests; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B)
claims.evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the fraction of Pdgfra+ OPs in the P14 subcortical white matter that immunolabelled for Ki67 between Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ mice.
claims.source: nor was there any difference in the fraction of Pdgfra+ OPs in the P14 SCWM that immunolabelled for Ki67, a marker of actively dividing cells (p=0.78, Student's t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunolabeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The OP division rate is not affected by loss of GluA2 and GluA3.
claims.source: These data indicate that the OP division rate is not affected by loss of GluA2 and GluA3.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU and Ki67 data.

claims.claim: The proportion of Olig2+ cells that labelled for cleaved Caspase-3 in Gria3null2+/+ controls at P14 was 22.7 ± 1.2%.
claims.source: The proportion of Olig2+ cells that labelled for cleaved Caspase-3 in Gria3null2+/+ controls at P14 was 22.7 ± 1.2% (n = 8 mice).
claims.evidence: Supported by cleaved Caspase-3 immunolabeling data.

claims.claim: In Gria3null2–/– mice, the cleaved Caspase-3-positive fraction was increased by a factor approximately 1.19 compared to controls.
claims.source: In Gria3null2–/– mice the cleaved Caspase-3-positive fraction was increased by a factor ~1.19 (increased by 19.4 ± 4.2%, p=0.002, Student's t-test with Welch's correction; Figure 7G,H.).
claims.evidence: Supported by cleaved Caspase-3 immunolabeling data shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: Some newly-forming Enpp6+ oligodendrocytes express one or more GluA subunits.
claims.source: We confirmed by double ISH for Enpp6 and Gria2, Gria3 or Gria4 that some newly-forming Enpp6+ OLs express one or more GluA subunits (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Signalling through AMPAR in oligodendrocyte lineage cells promotes survival of newly-differentiating oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that signalling through AMPAR in OL lineage cells promotes survival of newly-differentiating OLs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the increased apoptosis and reduced OL numbers.

claims.claim: There was a approximately 20% reduction in the number of myelin cross-sections in Gria3null2–/– normalized to littermate controls at P14.
claims.source: This revealed a ~20% reduction in the number of myelin cross-sections in Gria3null2–/– normalized to littermate controls at P14 (p=0.02, Mann-Whitney test), consistent with the ~27% reduction in the number of OLs in Gria3null2–/– mice at the same age (see previous section; Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: There was no change in the average length of internodes in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ at P14.
claims.source: There was no change in the average length of internodes (p=0.47, Student's t-test) or the average number of internodes per OL (p=0.26, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by dye-filling data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: There was no change in the average number of internodes per oligodendrocyte in Gria3null2–/– compared to Gria3null2+/+ at P14.
claims.source: There was no change in the average length of internodes (p=0.47, Student's t-test) or the average number of internodes per OL (p=0.26, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 8C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by dye-filling data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: At P70, there was no longer any significant difference in the number of myelin cross-sections per unit area observed by EM between Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2+/+ mice.
claims.source: At P70 there was no longer any significant difference in the number of myelin cross-sections per unit area observed by EM (p=0.57, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 8B), consistent with the fact that the numbers of OLs identified by CC1 immunolabelling were similar in Gria3null and Gria3null2–/– at this age (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Each oligodendrocyte synthesizes a similar total length of myelin sheath in Gria3null2–/– mice as in controls.
claims.source: Our data are consistent with a model in which each OL synthesizes a similar total length of myelin sheath in Gria3null2–/– mice as in controls and the overall synthesis of myelin is reduced in proportion to the reduced number of OLs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing proportional reduction in myelin and OLs.

claims.claim: The current density of kainate-evoked current in Gria3null2–/–4–/– was dramatically reduced to approximately 23% of that observed in Gria3null2–/– littermates.
claims.source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of YFP+ OPs in the P14 SCWM revealed that the current density of kainate-evoked current elicited by application of 100 µM kainate at –63 mV was dramatically reduced in Gria3null2–/–4–/– to ~23% of that observed in Gria3null2–/– littermates (p<10–4, Student's t-test with Welch correction; Figure 9A,B)
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Application of 50 μM GYKI blocked the kainate-evoked current in Gria3null2–/–4–/– only by approximately 39% as opposed to approximately 80% in Gria3null2–/–.
claims.source: In support of this, application of 50 μM GYKI blocked the kainate-evoked current in Gria3null2–/–4–/– only by ~39% as opposed to ~80% in Gria3null2–/– (p=0.005, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: The I-V relationship of the kainate-evoked current was nearly linear in Gria3null2–/–4–/– OPs, not inwardly-rectifying as in Gria3null2–/–.
claims.source: Moreover, the I-V relationship of the kainate-evoked current was nearly linear in Gria3null2–/–4–/– OPs, not inwardly-rectifying as in Gria3null2–/– (different rectification indices, p=0.005, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 9D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9D,E.

claims.claim: Almost no EPSCs were detected following application of 100 μM RR to brain slices from Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice.
claims.source: Consistent with the apparent lack of AMPAR in Gria3null2–/–4–/– OPs, and with AMPARs rather than KARs being the main receptor type activated at axon-OP synapses, almost no EPSCs were detected following application of 100 μM RR to brain slices (significantly less than in Gria3null2–/–; p=0.03, Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 9F,G).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9G.

claims.claim: AMPAR signalling is essentially abolished in Gria3null2–/–4–/– oligodendrocyte precursors.
claims.source: These data show that AMPAR signalling is essentially abolished in Gria3null2–/–4–/– OPs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claims.claim: At P14, there was a approximately 22% reduction in the density of oligodendrocytes in Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice relative to Gria3null controls.
claims.source: At P14 there was a ~22% reduction in the density of OLs relative to Gria3null controls and at p53 a ~26% reduction (p=0.026 at P14; p=0.029 at P53, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 10A,B)
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: At P53, there was a approximately 26% reduction in the density of oligodendrocytes in Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice relative to Gria3null controls.
claims.source: At P14 there was a ~22% reduction in the density of OLs relative to Gria3null controls and at p53 a ~26% reduction (p=0.026 at P14; p=0.029 at P53, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 10A,B)
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: There was no concomitant change in the density of OPs in Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice at P14 and P53.
claims.source: without a concomitant change in the density of OPs (p=0.11 at P14; p=0.7 at P53, Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 10C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: The fraction of Olig2+ cells that expressed cleaved Caspase-3 in subcortical white matter of P14 Gria3null controls was 24.8 ± 0.8%.
claims.source: The fraction of Olig2+ cells that expressed cleaved Caspase-3 in SCWM of P14 Gria3null controls was 24.8 ± 0.8% (n = 5 mice) and this increased in Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice by a factor of ~1.24 (increased by 24.2 ± 4.8%, p=0.004, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 10E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cleaved Caspase-3 immunolabeling data.

claims.claim: In Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice, the cleaved Caspase-3-positive fraction increased by a factor of approximately 1.24 compared to controls.
claims.source: The fraction of Olig2+ cells that expressed cleaved Caspase-3 in SCWM of P14 Gria3null controls was 24.8 ± 0.8% (n = 5 mice) and this increased in Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice by a factor of ~1.24 (increased by 24.2 ± 4.8%, p=0.004, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 10E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cleaved Caspase-3 immunolabeling data shown in Figure 10F.

claims.claim: There was no change in the length of the internodes or the number of internodes per oligodendrocyte in Gria3null2–/–4–/– compared to Gria3null mice.
claims.source: As observed for Gria3null2–/– mice, there was no significant change in the average length (p=0.93, Student's t-test) or number (p=0.41, Student's t-test) of internodes per individual Gria3null2–/–4–/– OL, analyzed by dye-filling OLs in brain slices (Figure 10G,H).
claims.evidence: Supported by dye-filling data shown in Figure 10H.

claims.claim: Signalling through AMPAR stimulates oligodendrocyte production and myelination in the white matter by enhancing survival of newly-formed oligodendrocytes, without a detectable effect on oligodendrocyte morphology.
claims.source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that signalling through AMPAR stimulates OL production and myelination in the white matter by enhancing survival of newly-formed OLs, without a detectable effect on OL morphology.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data.

claims.claim: The reduction in oligodendrocyte number observed in the Gria2/3 and Gria2/3/4 mutants results from an aspect of AMPAR signalling other than Ca2+ permeability.
claims.source: The fact that knockout of Gria2 alone did not affect OL development implies that the reduction in OL number observed in the Gria2/3 and Gria2/3/4 mutants results from an aspect of AMPAR signalling other than Ca2+ permeability, for example the induced depolarization or the Na+ influx that it produces.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the phenotypes of different knockout combinations.

claims.claim: AMPAR signalling in oligodendrocyte precursors and/or early-differentiating oligodendrocytes is a positive regulator of oligodendrocyte development.
claims.source: Thus, AMPAR signalling in OPs and/or early-differentiating OLs is a positive regulator of OL development; we speculate that this favours myelination of active axons that are releasing glutamate, thus accelerating development of a functioning CNS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion with a speculative component about the functional significance.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte lineage cells in the subcortical white matter express mRNA encoding AMPAR subunits GluA2, GluA3 and GluA4 but not GluA1.
claims.source: We have shown that OL lineage cells in the SCWM express mRNA encoding AMPAR subunits GluA2, GluA3 and GluA4 but not GluA1 - the same spectrum of AMPAR subunits reported for rat and mouse OPs in culture (Patneau et al., 1994; Zhang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by ISH data and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Knocking out GluA2 and GluA3 in oligodendrocyte precursors reduced the AMPAR-mediated current to approximately 53% of normal.
claims.source: Knocking out GluA2 and GluA3 in OPs reduced the AMPAR-mediated current to ~53% of normal, while knocking out all three subunits GluA2/3/4 reduced it to ~13% of normal.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 5 and 9.

claims.claim: Knocking out all three subunits GluA2/3/4 in oligodendrocyte precursors reduced the AMPAR-mediated current to approximately 13% of normal.
claims.source: Knocking out GluA2 and GluA3 in OPs reduced the AMPAR-mediated current to ~53% of normal, while knocking out all three subunits GluA2/3/4 reduced it to ~13% of normal.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figures 5 and 9.

claims.claim: In oligodendrocyte precursors lacking GluA2 and GluA3, the amplitude of RR-induced synaptic events was unchanged while their frequency was reduced to less than 30% of normal.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that in OPs lacking GluA2 and GluA3 the amplitude of RR-induced synaptic events was unchanged while their frequency was reduced to <30% of normal, while in OPs lacking all AMPAR subunits their frequency was reduced to only ~1% of control.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In oligodendrocyte precursors lacking all AMPAR subunits, the frequency of RR-induced synaptic events was reduced to only approximately 1% of control.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that in OPs lacking GluA2 and GluA3 the amplitude of RR-induced synaptic events was unchanged while their frequency was reduced to <30% of normal, while in OPs lacking all AMPAR subunits their frequency was reduced to only ~1% of control.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claims.claim: There are fewer AMPAR-containing synapses in double-knockout oligodendrocyte precursors and almost none in triple-knockouts.
claims.source: The simplest interpretation is that there are fewer AMPAR-containing synapses in double-KO OPs (and almost none in triple-KOs), but that those synapses that survive contain a normal number of AMPARs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the synaptic event frequency and amplitude data.

claims.claim: Almost all glutamatergic synaptic input to oligodendrocyte precursors is via AMPARs composed of GluA2, GluA3 and GluA4 subunits.
claims.source: In any case our data provide striking genetic confirmation that almost all glutamatergic synaptic input to OPs is via AMPARs composed of GluA2, GluA3 and GluA4 subunits.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic knockout data.

claims.claim: Oligodendrocyte precursor proliferation and OP number were normal in Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice.
claims.source: We found that OP proliferation and OP number were normal in Gria3null2–/– and Gria3null2–/–4–/– mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by cell counting and EdU incorporation data in Figures 7 and 10.

claims.claim: The reduced number of differentiated oligodendrocytes in the double- and triple-knockouts was a result of increased death of oligodendrocyte lineage cells.
claims.source: We found that the reduced number of differentiated OLs in the double- and triple-KOs was a result of increased death of OL lineage cells – most likely newly-formed, pre-myelinating OLs.
claims.evidence: Supported by cleaved Caspase-3 data in Figures 7 and 10.

claims.claim: Synaptic input and activation of AMPARs promotes neuronal survival during early postnatal development.
claims.source: Synaptic input – and activation of AMPARs in particular – has been shown to promote neuronal survival during early postnatal development (Heck et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Heck et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Sensory input from the whiskers to somatosensory barrel cortex promotes the survival of newly-differentiating oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: and a recent study showed that sensory input from the whiskers to somatosensory barrel cortex promotes the survival of newly-differentiating OLs (Hill et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hill et al., 2014.

claims.claim: AMPAR signalling in oligodendrocyte lineage cells could be one of the mechanisms ensuring that only pre-myelinating oligodendrocytes that make contact with active axons survive to myelinate in the longer term.
claims.source: Thus, AMPAR signalling in OL lineage cells could be one of the mechanisms ensuring that only pre-myelinating OLs that make contact with active axons survive to myelinate in the longer term (Barres et al., 1992, 1993; Trapp et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The amount of myelin in the subcortical white matter of Gria3null2–/– mice was reduced in proportion to the reduced number of oligodendrocytes.
claims.source: In our present study we found that the amount of myelin in the SCWM of Gria3null2–/– mice was reduced in proportion to the reduced number of OLs.
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The g-ratio, as well as the internode number and length, were unchanged in Gria3null2–/– mice.
claims.source: The g-ratio, as well as the internode number and length, were unchanged, suggesting that once a pre-myelinating OL makes a commitment to myelinate an axon, the process continues until a normal internode number and length, and a normal number of myelin wraps are achieved.
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy and dye-filling data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: AMPAR signalling stimulates myelin formation in mice by increasing the number of myelinating oligodendrocytes that develop from OPs, not by regulating myelin synthesis per se.
claims.source: In short, we have shown that AMPAR signalling stimulates myelin formation in mice by increasing the number of myelinating OLs that develop from OPs, not by regulating myelin synthesis per se.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: AMPAR signalling in oligodendrocyte lineage cells promotes oligodendrocyte development and myelination during postnatal development.
claims.source: In summary, our study demonstrates that AMPAR signalling in OL lineage cells promotes OL development and myelination during postnatal development.
claims.evidence: This is the summary conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: Approximately 80% of oligodendrocyte precursors in the postnatal subcortical white matter of wild type mice originate after birth from neural stem cells in the cortical ventricular zone.
claims.source: Most OPs (~80%) in the postnatal SCWM of wild type mice originate after birth (E21/P0) from neural stem cells in the cortical ventricular zone (VZ), with the remaining ~20% of OPs migrating into the developing cortex from the ventral forebrain starting around embryonic day 16 (E16) (Kessaris et al., 2006; Tripathi et al., 2011; reviewed by Bergles and Richardson, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Approximately 20% of oligodendrocyte precursors in the postnatal subcortical white matter migrate into the developing cortex from the ventral forebrain starting around embryonic day 16.
claims.source: Most OPs (~80%) in the postnatal SCWM of wild type mice originate after birth (E21/P0) from neural stem cells in the cortical ventricular zone (VZ), with the remaining ~20% of OPs migrating into the developing cortex from the ventral forebrain starting around embryonic day 16 (E16) (Kessaris et al., 2006; Tripathi et al., 2011; reviewed by Bergles and Richardson, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: AMPAR tetramers lacking GluA2 display inwardly-rectifying current responses to kainate and AMPA due to a voltage-dependent block of the channel by polyamines at positive potentials.
claims.source: AMPAR tetramers lacking GluA2 display inwardly-rectifying current responses to kainate and AMPA, due to a voltage-dependent block of the channel by polyamines at positive potentials (Donevan and Rogawski, 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Donevan and Rogawski, 1995.

claims.claim: When GluA2 is present in the edited 'R' form, the current-voltage relationship is linear, that is, non-rectifying.
claims.source: When GluA2 is present (in the edited 'R' form), the current-voltage (I-V) relationship is linear, that is, non-rectifying.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about AMPAR biophysics.

results.result: Oligodendrocyte lineage cells in subcortical white matter express AMPAR subunits GluA2, GluA3, and GluA4, but not GluA1. In situ hybridization showed that Gria2, Gria3, and Gria4 are expressed by many small cells in postnatal white matter, with 88-94% of Gria2-4+ cells co-expressing the oligodendrocyte lineage marker Olig2. Gria1 was expressed only by rare neurons in white matter.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C27-C33, and C93 are well-supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1 and 2, demonstrating specific AMPAR subunit expression patterns in oligodendrocyte lineage cells. The quantification of co-expression with Olig2 provides strong evidence for the cell-type specificity of this expression pattern.

results.result: Loss of GluA3 alone does not affect oligodendrocyte development or myelination. Gria3 germline knockout mice showed no changes in OP density, oligodendrocyte density, OP proliferation rate, or myelination at P14 and P21 compared to wild-type littermates.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C37-C40 are supported by cell counting, EdU incorporation, and electron microscopy data presented in Figure 3. Statistical tests showed no significant differences between Gria3null and wild-type mice across multiple developmental timepoints and measures of oligodendrocyte lineage development.

results.result: Conditional deletion of GluA2 in oligodendrocyte lineage cells using Sox10-Cre altered AMPAR calcium permeability but did not affect oligodendrocyte development. The rectification index was significantly reduced in Gria2−/− OPs, confirming successful deletion, but OP and oligodendrocyte densities and proliferation rates remained normal at P14.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4D-E) confirming altered AMPAR properties and cell counting data (Figure 4H-I) showing no changes in cell densities or proliferation. This demonstrates that calcium permeability through AMPARs is not critical for oligodendrocyte development.

results.result: Double deletion of GluA2 and GluA3 in oligodendrocyte lineage cells reduced AMPAR-mediated currents by approximately 47% without affecting basic membrane properties. Gria3null2−/− mice were viable without neurological signs, and the remaining AMPARs are likely GluA4 homo-tetramers, as Gria1 was not upregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C56 are supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5 showing reduced current density, maintained AMPAR-mediated responses (GYKI sensitivity), and unchanged membrane properties. ISH data (Figure 5—supplement 2) confirmed no compensatory Gria1 upregulation, supporting the inference about GluA4 homo-tetramers.

results.result: In Gria3null2−/− oligodendrocyte precursors, the amplitude of synaptic events was unchanged but their frequency was reduced to less than 30% of normal, suggesting fewer functional synapses rather than altered presynaptic release. The paired-pulse ratio was unchanged, supporting a postsynaptic mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61, C96, and C98 are supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6 showing preserved EPSC amplitude but dramatically reduced frequency in double-knockout OPs. The unchanged paired-pulse ratio (C60) provides strong evidence that the reduction reflects fewer synapses rather than altered presynaptic function, supporting the inference in C61 and C98.

results.result: Double deletion of GluA2/3 in oligodendrocyte lineage cells resulted in approximately 22-27% fewer oligodendrocytes during early postnatal development (P7-P14) due to increased apoptosis of newly-differentiating oligodendrocytes, without affecting OP proliferation or number. The oligodendrocyte deficit recovered by adulthood (P70).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C62-C73, C100-C101 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: CC1+ cell counts (Figure 7B), Enpp6+ newly-differentiating OL counts (Figure 7D), unchanged OP densities and proliferation (Figure 7F, Figure 7—supplement 1), and increased cleaved Caspase-3 expression (Figure 7H). The convergence of these data strongly supports the conclusion that AMPAR signaling promotes oligodendrocyte survival.

results.result: The oligodendrocyte deficit in Gria3null2−/− mice resulted in approximately 20% fewer myelin sheaths at P14, but the average length, number, and thickness of myelin internodes per oligodendrocyte were normal. By P70, myelin density recovered to control levels, consistent with recovery of oligodendrocyte numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C74-C78, C105-C106 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 8B) showing proportional reduction in myelin, dye-filling experiments (Figure 8C-D) showing normal internode parameters, and g-ratio measurements (Figure 8G-H) showing normal myelin thickness. The proportional relationship between oligodendrocyte and myelin reduction supports the inference that each oligodendrocyte produces normal amounts of myelin.

results.result: Triple deletion of GluA2/3/4 in oligodendrocyte lineage cells reduced AMPAR-mediated currents to approximately 13% of normal (23% of Gria3null2−/−), with the remaining current being predominantly kainate receptor-mediated. Synaptic events were nearly abolished, confirming that AMPARs composed of GluA2/3/4 mediate almost all glutamatergic synaptic input to OPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83, C95, C97 are strongly supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9 showing dramatically reduced current density, reduced GYKI sensitivity, linear I-V relationship (indicating non-AMPAR currents), and near-complete loss of synaptic events. This provides definitive genetic evidence for the AMPAR subunit composition at OP synapses.

results.result: Triple deletion of GluA2/3/4 resulted in approximately 22-26% fewer oligodendrocytes at both P14 and P53, with increased apoptosis but no change in OP density or internode morphology. Unlike the double knockout, the oligodendrocyte deficit persisted into adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C84-C89 are supported by cell counting data (Figure 10B, D), cleaved Caspase-3 measurements (Figure 10F), and dye-filling experiments (Figure 10H). The persistence of the oligodendrocyte deficit in triple knockouts, unlike the recovery seen in double knockouts, suggests that residual AMPAR signaling in double knockouts is sufficient for eventual recovery.

results.result: AMPAR-mediated signaling from active axons stimulates myelin production in developing white matter by enhancing oligodendrocyte survival, not by regulating myelin synthesis per se. This effect is independent of AMPAR calcium permeability and represents a positive regulatory mechanism that may favor myelination of active axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C90-C92, C99, C107-C108 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the convergence of multiple experimental results: genetic deletion of AMPAR subunits (C99), lack of phenotype in Gria2 single knockout (C91), increased apoptosis without changes in proliferation or myelin per cell (C90, C107), and normal development in Gria3 single knockout. The inference about favoring active axons (C92) is speculative but reasonable.

results.result: Background claims about myelin function: myelin enables fast and energy-efficient signal propagation by decreasing axonal capacitance, oligodendrocytes can transfer energy substrates to axons, and myelin synthesis requires substantial energy investment, suggesting evolutionary pressure to myelinate active rather than silent axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C11 are well-established facts in neuroscience supported by the cited literature. Claim C12 is a reasonable speculation based on the energy cost of myelination (C11), though it remains an inference rather than a demonstrated fact.

results.result: Prior literature review: electrical activity can modulate myelination through various mechanisms, oligodendrocyte lineage cells express glutamate receptors and receive synaptic input, and pharmacological or genetic manipulations of neurotransmitter signaling affect myelination, though results have been contradictory.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C26 accurately summarize prior published work as indicated by the citations. The authors appropriately note contradictions in the literature (e.g., C22 vs C23) and acknowledge that prior pharmacological approaches had limitations that motivated the current genetic approach.

results.result: Additional background and discussion claims: Gria2 germline knockouts show behavioral abnormalities and Gria2/3 double knockouts develop tremor; AMPAR signaling promotes neuronal survival; most OPs in postnatal white matter originate postnatally from cortical ventricular zone; AMPARs lacking GluA2 show inward rectification due to polyamine block.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C102-C104, C109-C112 are supported by the cited literature and represent established knowledge. These provide important context for interpreting the current results, particularly the inference that tremor in germline knockouts is not due to oligodendrocyte defects (C49) and the mechanistic basis for the electrophysiological measurements.
